extracted.intended_audience: writers and scholars of satire, translators, and readers studying Rabelaisian comic technique
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and analyze recurring stylistic devices and comedic techniques exemplified in this Rabelais passage (grotesque imagery, parody of institutions, neologisms, etc.), useful for writers emulating or scholars dissecting Renaissance satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grotesque bodily imagery and scatological humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent, explicit references to bodily functions and deformity (e.g. 'the last fart', 'shit-breech fellows', 'bursting', 'his very hose were watered', 'son of a bitch... with a pair of heads').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gross, physical detail and scatology to shock, debase pretension, and produce low-comic laughter; employ vivid, sensory language to amplify absurdity. Example anti-pattern: over-explaining the joke rather than letting the image carry the comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbole and extravagant scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Absurdly magnified descriptions and numbers (e.g. 'an infinite number of little pimping wine-presses', '7,532,810 huge drums', 'she was at least eighteen hundred years old').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply deliberate overstatement to make scenarios ludicrous and highlight satire; piling improbable magnitudes creates a surreal tone. Avoid subtle understatement when the comic aim is to overwhelm; hyperbole works by excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody of institutions and offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Mocking institutional roles and legal/bureaucratic language (e.g. contractors, 'Review' kept in chains, 'Twofold', 'Refusing-of-fees', 'their worships').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invent caricatured offices/titles and stage them performing grotesque or corrupt tasks to satirize real institutions. Use familiar institutional patina (formal titles, rituals) inverted for ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neologisms, invented technical-sounding terms, and lists of officious names
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous fabricated officer titles and pseudo-technical words (e.g. 'abstractors, spodizators, masticators, pregustics, tabachins, neemanins, rabrebans...' and odd compounds like 'bills-of-charge').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create playful, mock-technical vocabulary to lampoon learned jargon and to make the world feel simultaneously erudite and ridiculous. The crowding of odd names increases comic bewilderment; avoid making words so opaque the reader cannot follow the satire's target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing high/learned register with vulgarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Lofty, Latinate-sounding or scholarly phrasing is placed alongside crude bodily jokes and plain vulgarities (e.g. the queen's grandiloquent speech followed by 'Tabachins, a panacea' and immediate crude cures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juxtapose erudite diction and pretentious rhetoric with base imagery or actions to create contrast-based comedy and to deflate pretension. Keep the learned language plausibly pompous so the contrast stings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurd pseudo-medicine and parody of scientific/quack cures
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridiculous cures and pseudo-medical reasoning (e.g. cures 'with a song', wooden shoe touches, hanging a fox-tail, striking the belly with a hatchet, extracting water from pumice-stones).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invent implausible remedies and rituals that mimic medical discourse to satirize charlatanism and credulity. Present them with procedural detail to give them mock-authority; avoid realistic medical claims that might read as earnest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogues and comedic accumulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Long enumerations of people, cures, dances, offices, and actions (lists of dances, lists of officers and their absurd tasks, sequences of miraculous cures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use piling/lists to build momentum and comedic intensity—repetition plus variety increases absurdity. Vary items in the list for surprise (some plausible, some absurd). Watch for reader fatigue; lists should escalate or culminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic similes, metaphors, and unexpected comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Striking, often grotesque similes and metaphors (e.g. 'like an ass with squibs and crackers tied to its tail', 'like falling into Scylla to avoid Charybdis (out of the frying-pan into the fire)').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy unexpected or exaggerated comparisons to achieve instant comic images; combine classical/allusive references with vulgar comparisons for added effect. Avoid clichés that dilute surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical-situation comedy and slapstick scenarios
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot moments structured as pratfalls or physical mishaps (e.g. ships stranded on sands, towing by drums, a host 'bursting', whirlpools drenching a ship).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage sequences where physical complications and escalation create humor; visualize the chaos concretely. Use timing and piling of mishaps to heighten the farce; don't overexplain after the gag—let the scene speak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mock-ceremony, ritualized language, and symbolic gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalized but ludicrous court rituals and symbolic words (e.g. 'A panacea' as symbolic word, 'they colled and clipped us about the neck', elaborate ceremonial vocabulary used for trivial ends).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mimic ceremonial diction and ritual actions with mismatch between form and substance to satirize pomp and formality. Ritual language gains comic force when it serves a petty or ridiculous purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire of learned men, pseudo-philosophy, and pointless erudition
rubrics_metrics.description: Depictions of scholars engaged in absurd, trivial, or self-important tasks (e.g. sophists disputing over 'a he-ass’s shadow', measuring fleas for statecraft, philosophers turned idlers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray scholarly activity as disconnected from practical reality by giving it trivial objects and self-important framing; this exposes pretension and lampoons intellectual vanity. The more technical-sounding the pretension, the sharper the satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification and animated-inanimate absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributing living agency or social roles to inanimate objects and materials (e.g. organs 'pipes of cassia', drums that 'murmur' and are filled with sausages, 'Jupiter writes... on the dipthera or skin of the Amalthaean goat').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Animate objects with human-like roles and functions to intensify surreal comedy and to unsettle normal expectations. Use detailed, specific material images to ground the absurdity; avoid vagueness which lessens the comic image.
